name: Names the cumulative/per-interval categories vs. states what actually makes a KPISet cumulative
side_a: Credit when the answer states the defining property of a cumulative KPISet — that its data persists and keeps being appended to across the whole test run (as opposed to per-interval sets that are reset/recreated each second) — even if the words 'merge' or 'aggregate' never appear. The scope/lifetime statement is what counts as discussing the meaning.
side_b: Deduct when 'cumulative' appears only as a category label or contrast term (e.g., 'individual vs. cumulative KPIsets', 'restrict it to cumulative KPIsets') with no statement of what distinguishes it — no mention of spanning the whole run, accumulating samples, or persisting across intervals. Merely naming the two kinds is not discussing the meaning.

name: Answer never characterizes what a cumulative KPISet is (nothing to be wrong) vs answer volunteers a description of cumulative-set behavior
side_a: No deduction when the answer makes no substantive claim about the nature of cumulative KPISets — e.g. it only says the code treats all sets alike, or discusses compact_times() as a generic preprocessing/memory-optimization step without asserting how cumulative sets accumulate. Silence on the cumulative-set semantics cannot be a mischaracterization, so credit it.
side_b: Deduct the 3 points whenever the answer volunteers its own account of cumulative KPISet behavior (continuous accumulation of samples, unbounded growth of the response-time list, same list appended to across the run, contrasted with per-interval sets that reset), since that account departs from the correct 'merge of two or more KPISets' definition — even if the claim is hedged or only used as rationale.

name: Final recommendation restricts the call to cumulative sets only vs. recommends/permits calling it on every KPIset
side_a: no_deduct: the answer's actual recommendation is exclusive — compact_times() is called ONLY on cumulative KPIsets, and per-interval sets are explicitly excluded from the call.
side_b: deduct: the answer's operative recommendation is to call compact_times() on every KPIset (even if it concedes it is only 'strictly required' or 'mandatory' for cumulative ones), or defers to the current code's uniform behavior.

name: Asserts compacting per-interval sets is actively undesirable vs. asserts it is harmless/free
side_a: no_deduct: the answer gives a positive reason not to compact non-cumulative sets (loses needed per-interval data / resets each interval anyway), treating the call as inappropriate there.
side_b: deduct: the answer characterizes compacting non-cumulative sets as harmless, cheap, a no-op, or a consistency nicety, so nothing rules out applying it everywhere.

name: Framing _compact_times() as a prerequisite that recalculate()/metric computation depends on vs as an independent housekeeping step
side_a: No deduct when the answer treats _compact_times() as an independent, self-contained operation on the stored times (it bounds the list / returns early when small) and never asserts that the rest of recalculate() depends on it having run — i.e. no claim that the data must be 'prepared', 'preprocessed' or 'already compacted' before metrics are produced.
side_b: Deduct the 2 points whenever the answer asserts an ordering/data dependency — that recalculate() assumes or requires compacted data, that compaction is a 'necessary preprocessing step', or that it 'prepares the data' for subsequent calculations — since this invents a dependency that does not exist; the step is purely a size-bounding optimisation that the rest of recalculate() does not rely on.

name: Compacting a per-interval set is a harmless no-op vs it would destroy data still needed
side_a: No deduct when the answer explains that for small/per-interval sets compaction simply does nothing (early return, harmless, merely unnecessary) — this matches the threshold guard in the real method.
side_b: Deduct the 2 points when the answer claims that compacting a per-interval KPIset would be destructive — e.g. that it 'would discard information you still need' for that interval's statistics — since this misstates both the guard behaviour and the effect of compaction on the interval's reported metrics.

name: Treats the repeated call as a real performance concern (worth measuring) vs. explicitly dismisses it as harmless/cheap
side_a: No deduction when the answer treats the repeated invocation as a genuine performance concern — i.e., it flags a possible performance impact and/or recommends profiling/measuring before deciding. Credit is given even if the answer ultimately keeps the call on every KPISet, because it acknowledges there is something costly to weigh.
side_b: Deduct when the answer affirmatively neutralizes the cost — saying the call is 'harmless', 'inexpensive', 'returns immediately', or otherwise asserting there is no penalty to calling it everywhere. Explicitly denying overhead cannot count as identifying overhead.

name: Locates the burden in performing the call vs. only in the data growth that compaction prevents
side_a: No deduction when the burden discussed is attributable to executing _compact_times itself (runtime/performance impact of invoking it on every KPISet), so the trade-off is 'calling it costs something'.
side_b: Deduct when the only resource talk is about the benefit side — unbounded response-time lists, memory growth, percentile computation being 'manageable' — i.e., what compaction saves rather than what running it costs. Framing compaction purely as a memory-saving necessity does not identify a cost of invoking it.
